chief_complaint: sudden, explosive thunderclap headache—the worst of her life
hpi_details: A 62-year-old female presents with a sudden, explosive thunderclap headache that reached maximal intensity within seconds and is the worst headache of her life.
ideas: She thinks a major blood vessel has ruptured in her head or that she is having a catastrophic stroke.
concerns: She is worried that she is having a massive brain bleed and might lose consciousness, suffer severe brain damage, or die.
expectations: She hopes to receive immediate intravenous pain relief and an emergency CT scan of her head.

investigation_events.title: Emergency CT and CT angiography
investigation_events.availability_message: Emergency CT and angiographic results are now available. Stroke and neurosurgical care should proceed immediately.

results.value: Acute subarachnoid hemorrhage within the basal cisterns and right Sylvian fissure
6 mm ruptured right middle cerebral artery bifurcation aneurysm

clinical_knowledge.topic: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (ruptured aneurysm) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (ruptured aneurysm) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: Emergent head CT without contrast, CT angiogram, coiling/clipping, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden, explosive thunderclap headache—the worst of her life
Key HPI features: A 62-year-old female presents with a sudden, explosive thunderclap headache that reached maximal intensity within seconds and is the worst headache of her life.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (ruptured aneurysm).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Thunderclap migraine without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Declining consciousness.
management_principles: Plan for Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: Emergent head CT without contrast, CT angiogram, coiling/clipping
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: Did the headache reach its peak within seconds?
Is this the worst headache of your life?

history.answer: Doctor, my head feels like it just exploded; it came on out of nowhere and it is the worst pain I have ever felt.
It struck instantly about two hours ago, reaching full peak intensity within just a couple of seconds like a thunderclap.
It started two hours ago and has not let up for even a second. I have never had a headache like this in my life.
It started intensely at the back of my head and neck, but now my entire skull feels like it is bursting open.
It feels like an explosive, tearing pressure inside my skull, easily a ten out of ten.
It has remained at ten out of ten constantly since the exact moment it struck two hours ago.
Any slight movement, bending my neck, or opening my eyes to bright light makes the throbbing much worse, and nothing helps.
No, there were no flashing lights, blind spots, or tingling beforehand; I felt completely normal until it hit.
Yes, I have severe nausea and threw up twice on the way here, and the room lights and voices hurt terribly.
No, my eyes are not tearing or red, my eyelid is not drooping, and my nose is not running.
I have not felt feverish or had chills, but my neck feels completely stiff and locked up.
I do not have any weakness or numbness in my arms or legs, but I felt dazed and lightheaded when it first struck.
My vision is slightly blurry from the sheer pain and light sensitivity, but I am not seeing double.
No, my temples are not tender, I have no pain when chewing food, and my shoulders and hips do not ache.
No, I did not fall, hit my head, or have any kind of accident.
My husband gave me two tablets of acetaminophen an hour ago, but they did not touch the pain at all.
I was lifting a heavy basket of laundry and straining when it suddenly struck my head.
I have never been told I have high blood pressure, and I do not take any blood thinners or daily medications.
No, my husband is at home and feels completely fine, and we do not use any gas space heaters.
No, I have never had cancer, HIV, or any problems with my immune system.
I have generally been very healthy and have no chronic illnesses.
I had an appendectomy when I was a teenager, but I have not had any surgeries or hospital stays since.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements regularly.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink a single glass of wine occasionally on special social occasions.
I am a retired elementary school teacher and live comfortably at home with my husband.
My mother tragically died suddenly in her early fifties from a burst brain aneurysm.
It felt like an explosion went off inside my skull, like a blood vessel suddenly burst.
I'm terrified that I'm going to pass out, suffer permanent brain damage, or not survive this.
I need urgent IV pain relief to stop this agony right now and an emergency scan of my brain.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 162/96 mmHg, pulse 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
The patient is lying still in bed with eyes closed in distress, grimacing and clutching her head.
Alert and fully oriented to person, place, and time, but slow to respond due to agonizing head pain.
Marked resistance and neck stiffness upon passive flexion, with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Pupils are equal, round, and briskly reactive to light; fundoscopy reveals clear optic disc margins without papilledema.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with full extraocular movements and no facial asymmetry.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with 5/5 strength throughout all four extremities.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation symmetrically throughout the upper and lower extremities.
Biceps, patellar, and Achilles reflexes are 2+ bilaterally, and plantar responses are flexor.
No tenderness over the frontal or maxillary sinuses, and temporal arteries are soft, pulsatile, and non-tender.
